To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The application of hog-manure on pastureland increased GHG emissions from cow-calf production systems.
the application of hog manue on grassland showed mean emission increases of 7.9 kg CO2-e/ kg liveweight and 8.5 kg CO2-e/kg liveweight in the CCM and IFSM, respectively.
The application of hog (pig) manure on grasslands increased the GHG emission intensity of a Canadian cow-c calf beef production system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of GHG mitigation strategies for beef production systems.
the development of whole-farm models that can be applied for assessing the impact of beneficial management practices on farm productivity and environmental sustainability.
the evaluation of greenhouse gas (GH) emissions from hog manure application in cow-calf beef production system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the application of hog manue on pasture in a cow-calf production systems increases GHG emissions.

the use of whole-farm modelling is a useful tool to evaluate the environmental impact of manure management practices in a beef cattle production system, but the accuracy and robustness of the models need further improvement.
the application of hog manue on grassland increased farm GHG emissions and that the environmental advantage of split application over single application was not consistent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the application of hog manures to grassland can reduce GHG intensity by increasing farm productivity.

the use of hog manure in cow–calf operations is a good practice to reduce GHG emission intensity, but there is still a need for a better understanding of the environmental impact of hog manure use in beef production systems.
the use of hog manure in a cow-calf production systems has little impact on the farm GHG intensity and the use of hog in split application is not environmentally advantageous.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the application of hog manures in cow-calf production systems in Canada can be a viable option to reduce farm GHG emissions.
whole-farm modeling can be a useful tool to evaluate the impact on farm productivity and emissions of manure management strategies.
the timing of manure application is not the most effective strategy to reduce GHG emissions from cow–calf systems.
